# utf8_ranges - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/utf8-ranges/

## Expand description

Crate `utf8-ranges` converts ranges of Unicode scalar values to equivalent
ranges of UTF-8 bytes. This is useful for constructing byte based automatons
that need to embed UTF-8 decoding.

See the documentation on the `Utf8Sequences` iterator for more details and
an example.

[§](https://docs.rs#wait-what-is-this)Wait, what is this?

This is simplest to explain with an example. Let’s say you wanted to test
whether a particular byte sequence was a Cyrillic character. One possible
scalar value range is `[0400-04FF]`. The set of allowed bytes for this
range can be expressed as a sequence of byte ranges:

This is simple enough: simply encode the boundaries, `0400` encodes to
`D0 80` and `04FF` encodes to `D3 BF`, and create ranges from each
corresponding pair of bytes: `D0` to `D3` and `80` to `BF`.

However, what if you wanted to add the Cyrillic Supplementary characters to
your range? Your range might then become `[0400-052F]`. The same procedure
as above doesn’t quite work because `052F` encodes to `D4 AF`. The byte ranges
you’d get from the previous transformation would be `[D0-D4][80-AF]`. However,
this isn’t quite correct because this range doesn’t capture many characters,
for example, `04FF` (because its last byte, `BF` isn’t in the range `80-AF`).

Instead, you need multiple sequences of byte ranges:

This gets even more complicated if you want bigger ranges, particularly if
they naively contain surrogate codepoints. For example, the sequence of byte
ranges for the basic multilingual plane (`[0000-FFFF]`) look like this:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
[0-7F]
[C2-DF][80-BF]
[E0][A0-BF][80-BF]
[E1-EC][80-BF][80-BF]
[ED][80-9F][80-BF]
[EE-EF][80-BF][80-BF]
```
Note that the byte ranges above will *not* match any erroneous encoding of
UTF-8, including encodings of surrogate codepoints.

And, of course, for all of Unicode (`[000000-10FFFF]`):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
[0-7F]
[C2-DF][80-BF]
[E0][A0-BF][80-BF]
[E1-EC][80-BF][80-BF]
[ED][80-9F][80-BF]
[EE-EF][80-BF][80-BF]
[F0][90-BF][80-BF][80-BF]
[F1-F3][80-BF][80-BF][80-BF]
[F4][80-8F][80-BF][80-BF]
```
This crate automates the process of creating these byte ranges from ranges of Unicode scalar values.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-would-i-ever-use-this)Why would I ever use this?

You probably won’t ever need this. In 99% of cases, you just decode the byte sequence into a Unicode scalar value and compare scalar values directly. However, this explicit decoding step isn’t always possible. For example, the construction of some finite state machines may benefit from converting ranges of scalar values into UTF-8 decoder automata (e.g., for character classes in regular expressions).

[§](https://docs.rs#lineage)Lineage

I got the idea and general implementation strategy from Russ Cox in his
[article on regexps](https://web.archive.org/web/20160404141123/https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp3.html) and RE2.
Russ Cox got it from Ken Thompson’s `grep` (no source, folk lore?).
I also got the idea from
[Lucene](https://github.com/apache/lucene-solr/blob/ae93f4e7ac6a3908046391de35d4f50a0d3c59ca/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/util/automaton/UTF32ToUTF8.java),
which uses it for executing automata on their term index.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Range.html)- Range
- A single inclusive range of UTF-8 bytes.
- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Sequences.html)- Sequences
- An iterator over ranges of matching UTF-8 byte sequences.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/enum.Utf8Sequence.html)- Sequence
- Utf8Sequence represents a sequence of byte ranges.

                                SIM workspace package for sim lib numbers tensor i64.

# utf8-ranges 1.0.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/utf8-ranges/latest

**DEPRECATED:** This crate has been folded into the
[ regex-syntax](https://docs.rs/regex-syntax) and is now deprecated.

# utf8-ranges

This crate converts contiguous ranges of Unicode scalar values to UTF-8 byte ranges. This is useful when constructing byte based automata from Unicode. Stated differently, this lets one embed UTF-8 decoding as part of one's automaton.

Dual-licensed under MIT or the [UNLICENSE](http://unlicense.org).

### Documentation

### Example

This shows how to convert a scalar value range (e.g., the basic multilingual plane) to a sequence of byte based character classes.

```
extern crate utf8_ranges;
use Utf8Sequences;
```
The output:

```
[0-7F]
[C2-DF][80-BF]
[E0][A0-BF][80-BF]
[E1-EC][80-BF][80-BF]
[ED][80-9F][80-BF]
[EE-EF][80-BF][80-BF]
```
These ranges can then be used to build an automaton. Namely:

- Every arbitrary sequence of bytes matches exactly one of the sequences of ranges or none of them.
- Every match sequence of bytes is guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. (Erroneous encodings of surrogate codepoints in UTF-8 cannot match any of the byte ranges above.)

---

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# yerba 0.7.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yerba/0.7.3

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/yerba/0.7.3/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

## What is Yerba?

Yerba is a lossless YAML editing tool. It lets you programmatically read, modify, and enforce formatting in YAML files while preserving their original structure, including comments, blank lines, quote styles, and key ordering.

Most YAML libraries parse a file into a data structure and serialize it back, discarding all formatting in the process. Yerba operates on the concrete syntax tree (CST), so your edits are surgical: only the targeted values change, and everything else stays exactly as it was.

Yerba is available as:

- A **standalone CLI binary**with zero runtime dependencies
- A **Rust crate**for embedding in Rust applications
- A **Ruby gem**for programmatic YAML editing from Ruby

Yerba was born out of the need to manage, validate, and enforce consistent formatting for hundreds of YAML data files in the [RubyEvents.org](https://github.com/rubyevents/rubyevents) project.

## Installation

### CLI (standalone)

The `yerba` CLI is a standalone Rust binary with no Ruby dependency. Install it via Cargo:

```
```
### Rust Crate

Use `yerba` as a library in your Rust project:

```
[]
 = "0.7"
```
```
let mut document = parse_file?;
document.set?;
document.save?;                  // saves to original path
document.save_to?;   // saves to new path
```
### Ruby Gem

The Ruby gem bundles both the CLI binary and a native extension for programmatic access from Ruby:

```
```
Or add it to your `Gemfile`:

```
```
The gem ships with precompiled binaries for macOS and Linux.

If no precompiled binary is available for your platform, it will compile from source automatically, which requires a [Rust toolchain](https://rustup.rs).

## CLI Usage

The `yerba` CLI follows a consistent pattern:

```
yerba <command> <file> <selector> [value] [options]
```
Selectors use dot-notation for nested keys, brackets for array access, and support glob patterns for operating on multiple files at once.

### Selectors

Selectors let you address any node in a YAML document:

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | A single key | `"database.host"` |
| `key.nested` | Nested key path | `"database.settings.pool"` |
| `[]` | All items in array | `"[].title"` |
| `[N]` | Item at index | `"[0].title"` |
| `[].key[].nested` | Nested array access | `"[].speakers[].name"` |

### Conditions

Conditions filter which items a command operates on:

| Syntax | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `.key == value` | Equality | `".kind == keynote"` |
| `.key != value` | Inequality | `".status != draft"` |
| `.key contains val` | Substring or member | `".title contains Ruby"` |
| `.key not_contains val` | Negated contains | `".title not_contains test"` |

`get`

Retrieve values from YAML files. Supports single values, array traversal, glob patterns across multiple files, conditions for filtering, and field selection.

```
```
Use `--select` to pick specific fields from each item, and `--condition` to filter which items are returned:

```
```
Glob patterns let you query across many files at once:

```
```
Use `--raw` to output plain values (one per line) instead of JSON:

```
```
`set`

Update an existing value at a path. The original quote style is preserved automatically, if a value was double-quoted before, it stays double-quoted after the edit.

```
```
Use `--if-exists` to only set the value when the path already exists, or `--if-missing` to only set it when the path does not exist:

```
```
Use `--condition` to only apply the change when a sibling field matches:

```
```
Use `--all` to update all nodes matching a wildcard selector:

```
```
`insert`

Insert a new key into a map or a new item into a sequence. By default, new items are appended at the end.

```
```
Control placement with `--before`, `--after`, or `--at`:

```
```
For sequences of maps, use conditions to position relative to other items:

```
```

```

`delete`

Remove a key and its value from a map:

Remove a specific item from a sequence by its value:

```

Rename a key in a map while preserving its value and position:

`move`

Move a sequence item to a new position. You can reference items by value, index, or condition:

```

`move-key`

Move a key to a new position within a map:

`sort`

Sort items in a sequence. For simple scalar sequences, no options are needed. For sequences of maps, use `--by` to specify the sort field. Use `--order desc` for descending. Repeat `--by` and `--order` for tie-breakers:

```
```
Use `--order` with a comma-separated list to specify an explicit custom order. All items must be listed:

```
```
This is useful for reordering items in a specific sequence (e.g., conference schedule order, priority lists) or when an LLM agent needs to rearrange items programmatically.

`sort-keys`

Reorder the keys in a map to match a predefined order. If any key in the document is not present in the order list, the command aborts with an error, this ensures you account for every field:

```
```
`quote-style`

Enforce a consistent quote style across keys and/or values:

```
```
Scope the operation to a specific selector:

```
```
Use block scalar styles to enforce multiline formatting on specific fields:

```
```
**Key styles** (`--keys`):

| Style | Symbol | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `plain` | — | `host: value` |
| `single` | `'` | `'host': value` |
| `double` | `"` | `"host": value` |

**Value styles** (`--values`):

| Style | Symbol | Example | Behavior | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `plain` | — | `host: localhost` | Unquoted | |
| `single` | `'` | `host: 'localhost'` | Single-quoted | |
| `double` | `"` | `host: "localhost"` | Double-quoted, supports `\n`escapes | |
| `literal` | `\ | -` | Preserves newlines | Strip trailing newline |
| `literal-clip` | `\ | ` | Preserves newlines | Keep one trailing newline |
| `literal-keep` | `\ | +` | Preserves newlines | Keep all trailing newlines |
| `folded` | `>-` | Folds newlines to spaces | Strip trailing newline | |
| `folded-clip` | `>` | Folds newlines to spaces | Keep one trailing newline | |
| `folded-keep` | `>+` | Folds newlines to spaces | Keep all trailing newlines |

Block scalars are only converted when scoped to a specific selector. An unscoped `--values double` will not touch existing block scalars.

`blank-lines`

Enforce a consistent number of blank lines between sequence entries:

```
```
`directives`

Add or remove the document start marker (`---`):

```
```
`unique`

Find or remove duplicate items in a sequence. Use `--by` to specify which field determines uniqueness:

```
```
By default, duplicates are reported but not removed. Use `--remove` to remove them (keeps the first occurrence):

```
```

Show the location (line, column, byte offset) of a selector in a YAML file:

```

```

Validate YAML files against a JSON schema:

```
```

`selectors`

Show all valid selectors for a YAML file. Useful for discovering the structure of a file and knowing which selectors you can use with other commands:

```
```

For sequences of objects:

`Yerbafile`

A `Yerbafile` is a YAML configuration file that defines formatting and editing rules as pipelines of operations that are applied to your files across your project.

Use `yerba init` to create one, then `yerba apply` to apply all rules, or `yerba check` to verify compliance (exits with code `1` if files would change):

```
```
A Yerbafile supports a global `pipeline` that runs on all matching files, plus per-rule pipelines for file-specific steps. Global steps run first, then per-rule steps refine or override:

```
files: "data/**/*.yml"
pipeline:
  - directives:
      max: 1
      ensure: true
  - collection_style:
      style: block
  - sequence_indent:
      style: indented
  - quote_style:
      key_style: plain
      value_style: double
rules:
  - files: "data/**/videos.yml"
    pipeline:
      - quote_style:
          path: "[].speakers"
          value_style: plain
      - sort_keys:
          path: "[]"
          order:
            - id
            - title
            - speakers
  - files: "data/speakers.yml"
    pipeline:
      - sort_keys:
          path: "[]"
          order:
            - name
            - slug
            - github
      - sort:
          by: name
```
Available pipeline steps:

- `quote_style`Enforce quote style on keys and/or values, optionally scoped by path
- `collection_style`Enforce flow or block style on collections
- `sequence_indent`Enforce compact or indented sequence style
- `sort_keys`Reorder keys to match a predefined list
- `sort`Sort sequence items by field(s)
- `blank_lines`Enforce blank lines between sequence entries
- `set`Set a value (supports conditions)
- `insert`Insert a new key or sequence item
- `delete`Remove a key (supports conditions)
- `rename`Rename a key
- `remove`Remove an item from a sequence
- `directives`Add or remove the document start marker (- `---`), with optional- `max`validation
- `unique`Find or remove duplicate items in a sequence
- `schema`Validate against a JSON schema (with optional- `path`for scoping)

This makes it easy to enforce project-wide YAML conventions in CI:

```
```
## Ruby API

Yerba includes a native C extension (backed by the same Rust core) that provides a full Ruby API for YAML editing.

### Parsing

Create a document from a file path or from a string:

```
document = Yerba.parse_file()
document = Yerba.parse()
```
### Creating Documents

Build documents from Ruby objects:

```
document = Yerba::Document.from({ name: , tags: [, ] })
document = Yerba::Document.from([{ id: , title:  }])
```
Build incrementally using `Document.new` and `root=`:

```
document = Yerba::Document.new
document.root = {}
document[] =
document[] =
document[] = [, ]
document[] = { host: , port: 5432 }
document.save_to!()
```
```
---
name: Event 123
kind: conference
tags:
  - ruby
  - rails
config:
  host: localhost
  port: 5432
```
Or start with `Document.from` and keep building:

```
document = Yerba::Document.from({ name:  })
document[] = []
document[] <<
document[] <<
```
Build a sequence document and append entries:

```
document = Yerba::Document.new
document.root = []
document << { id: , title: , speakers: [] }
document << { id: , title: , speakers: [, ] }
document.save_to!()
```
`document["key"]` and `document << item` are shortcuts for `document.root["key"]` and `document.root << item`.

### Reading Values

Use bracket notation (`[]`) to navigate the document. Returns typed node objects (`Scalar`, `Map`, or `Sequence`) that are live references — mutations flow back to the document.

All access methods (`[]`, `fetch`, `dig`, `value_at`) accept full selector strings like `"database.host"`, `"[0].title"`, or `"[].speakers[].name"`. In the examples below we prefer the more idiomatic chained bracket style, but the two forms are equivalent:

```
document[][].value  # => "localhost"
document[].value     # => "localhost" (same thing)
```
The returned object type depends on what's at the path:

```
document[]          # => Yerba::Map
document[][]  # => Yerba::Scalar
document[]              # => Yerba::Sequence
```
Scalars expose their value and quote style:

```
scalar = document[][]
scalar.value        # => "localhost"
scalar.quote_style  # => :double
```
Use `fetch` for strict access, it raises `Yerba::SelectorNotFoundError` with "did you mean?" suggestions if the selector doesn't exist:

```
document.fetch()  # => Yerba::Scalar
document.fetch()   # => raises SelectorNotFoundError: ... Did you mean: database.host?
```
Use `dig` to traverse multiple levels, returning `nil` for missing paths:

```
document.dig(, )     # => Yerba::Scalar
document.dig(, 0, )     # => Yerba::Scalar
document.dig(, )  # => nil
```
Use `value_at` to get the plain Ruby value (String, Integer, Hash, Array, etc.) instead of a node object:

```
document.value_at()  # => "localhost"
document.value_at()  # => 5432
document.value_at()       # => {"host" => "localhost", "port" => 5432}
document.value_at()       # => ["First Talk", "Second Talk"]
```
Summary of access methods:

| Method | Not found | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `[]` | `nil` | `Scalar`/`Map`/`Sequence`node |
| `fetch` | raises `SelectorNotFoundError` | `Scalar`/`Map`/`Sequence`node |
| `dig` | `nil` | `Scalar`/`Map`/`Sequence`node |
| `value_at` | `nil` | plain Ruby value |

### Mutations

Modify values in place. The original formatting is preserved:

```
document[][].value =
document.set(, 3306)
```
Set all matching nodes at once with `all: true`:

```
document.set(, , all: true)
```
Insert new keys with positional control:

```
document[].insert(, true, after: )
```
Set arrays and hashes as values, they default to block style:

```
document[][] = [, ]
# tags:
#   - ruby
#   - rails
document[][] = { pool: 5, timeout: 30 }
# settings:
#   pool: 5
#   timeout: 30
```
Use `set` with `style: :flow` for inline formatting:

```
document.root.set(, [, ], style: :flow)
# tags: [ruby, rails]
```
Work with sequences using familiar Ruby patterns:

```
tags = document[]
tags <<
tags << { name: , version:  }
tags.remove()
```
### Sorting

Sort sequences in place. Works on both the document and sequence level:

```
document.sort(by: :name)
document.sort(by: :name, order: :desc)
document.sort(by: :name, order: [, , ])
document.sort()
document.sort(, order: :desc)
document.sort(, order: [, , ])
```
The `by:` option accepts symbols, strings, or dot-prefixed strings (`:name`, `"name"`, `".name"`).

### Querying

Find and filter items in sequences with `find_by`, `where`, and `pluck`:

```
document.find_by(name: )
document.where(role: )
document.pluck(:name)
document.find_by(speakers: { name:  })
document.where(tags: [])
document.find_by(: )
```
These methods work on `Document` (delegates to root), `Sequence`, and `Collection` (searches across files):

```
collection = Yerba.files()
collection.find_by(name: )
collection.where(kind: )
collection.pluck(:name)
```
### Schema Validation

Validate documents against JSON schemas from Ruby:

```
schema = {
  type: ,
  properties: { name: { type:  }, slug: { type:  } },
  required: [, ]
}
document.valid?(schema)                 # => true/false
document.valid?(schema, selector: ) # validate each array item
errors = document.validate(schema, selector: )
errors.each do
  puts
end
```
Also accepts a JSON string:

```
document.valid?()
```
### Quote Style Control

Read and set the quote style on individual scalars:

```
scalar = document[][]
scalar.quote_style # => :double
scalar.quote_style = :single
```
### Collection Style

Read and change how collections are rendered, flow (inline) or block (multi-line):

```
document[].collection_style          # => :block or :flow
document[].collection_style = :flow  # => tags: [ruby, rails]
document[].collection_style = :block # => tags:\n  - ruby\n  - rails
```
Works on both sequences and maps:

```
document[].collection_style = :flow  # => database: {host: localhost, port: 5432}
document[].collection_style = :block # => database:\n  host: localhost\n  port: 5432
```
### Sequence Indent

Control whether sequence items are indented under their key or at the same level:

```
document[].sequence_indent             # => :indented or :compact
document[].sequence_indent = :compact  # compact style
document[].sequence_indent = :indented # indented style
```
```
# :compact               # :indented
tags:                    tags:
- ruby                     - ruby
- rails                    - rails
```
### Location

Get the precise location (line, column, byte offset) of any selector in a document:

```
loc = document[0][].location
loc.start_line    # => 2
loc.start_column  # => 9
loc.end_line      # => 2
loc.end_column    # => 19
loc.start_offset  # => 22
loc.end_offset    # => 32
```
You can also get a location by selector string:

```
document.location()
```
The above is the same as:

```
document[0][].location
document[].location
```
Omit the selector to get the whole document's location:

```
document.location # => #<Yerba::Location start_line=1, ...>
```
Returns `nil` for non-existent selectors. Use `locations` for wildcard selectors that match multiple nodes:

```
locs = document.locations()
locs.each {  puts  }
# line 2
# line 4
document.locations()
document.locations()
```
### Wildcard Access

When `[]` receives a wildcard selector (containing `[]`), it returns an array of nodes instead of a single node:

```
document[]       # => [Yerba::Scalar, Yerba::Scalar, ...]
document[]  # => [Yerba::Scalar, Yerba::Scalar, ...]
document[]   # => [Yerba::Scalar, Yerba::Scalar, ...]
document[].each {  puts scalar.value }
document[].each {  scalar.value =  }
```
### Collections

Operate on multiple files matching a glob pattern:

```
collection = Yerba.files()
collection.each do
  puts document[0][].value
end
collection.find_by(name: )
collection.where(kind: )
collection.pluck(:name)
collection.apply! do
  document.set(, )
end
```
Use `Collection.get` to retrieve nodes across all matching files in parallel. Returns `Scalar`, `Map`, or `Sequence` objects with `file_path`, `line`, and `selector`:

```
speakers = Yerba::Collection.get(, )
speakers.each do
  puts
end
maps = Yerba::Collection.get(, )
maps.first.class
# => Yerba::Map
sequences = Yerba::Collection.get(, )
sequences.first.class
# => Yerba::Sequence
```
Nodes returned by `Collection.get` lazily load their `Document` on first mutation, so reads are fast and writes work transparently:

```
scalars = Yerba::Collection.get(, )
scalars.first.value =
scalars.first.document.save!
```
### Saving

Write changes back to the original file:

```
document.save!
```
Save to a new path:

```
document.save_to!()
```
Or render the document as a string without writing to disk:

```
document.to_s
```

# hanzo-kernel 0.2.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.4

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.4/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

hanzo-kernel: Hanzo's first-party GPU kernel DSL.

Write a kernel ONCE in Rust; it lowers to CUDA / ROCm / Vulkan / Metal. This crate is the
first-party facade over the CubeCL lowering engine: kernel source names only `hanzo_kernel::*`,
never `cubecl`. "Values, not places" -- CubeCL is the implementation value; `hanzo_kernel` is the
stable namespace we build against, so the engine can be upgraded (or forked) without touching a
single kernel.

The perf primitives our hand-tuned kernels rely on are all here and lower to the native instruction on each backend:

- `dot`on a vectorized- `Line<i8>`-> dp4a / OpSDotAccSat (int8 4-way dot)
- `cmma`-> tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup)
- `SharedMemory`,- `plane_*`(subgroup reduce/shuffle),- `Atomic`, barriers

MIGRATION POLICY (perf-gated, never a downgrade): the DSL provides COVERAGE -- every quant type on every backend, from one source, killing the "same op, N impls, N numeric behaviors" bug class. A hand-tuned kernel is replaced by its DSL twin ONLY when the DSL version is bit-exact AND within perf noise (bench-gated). Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the specialized peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for the backends that lack a tuned version.

# westend_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/westend-runtime/35.0.0/westend_runtime/

## Expand description

The Westend runtime. This can be compiled with `#[no_std]`, ready for Wasm.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [api](https://docs.rs/api/index.html)
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_params/index.html)- params
- Dynamic params that can be adjusted at runtime.
- [fast_](https://docs.rs/fast_runtime_binary/index.html)- runtime_ - binary
- [migrations](https://docs.rs/migrations/index.html)
- The runtime migrations per release.
- [xcm_](https://docs.rs/xcm_config/index.html)- config
- XCM configurations for Westend.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_elections_weights.html)- elections_ - weights
- Implements the weight types for the elections module and a specific
runtime.
This macro should not be called directly; use
`impl_runtime_weights`

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [AVERAGE_](https://docs.rs/constant.AVERAGE_ON_INITIALIZE_RATIO.html)- ON_ - INITIALIZE_ - RATIO
- We assume that an on-initialize consumes 1% of the weight on average, hence a single extrinsic
will not be allowed to consume more than `AvailableBlockRatio - 1%`.
- [BABE_](https://docs.rs/constant.BABE_GENESIS_EPOCH_CONFIG.html)- GENESIS_ - EPOCH_ - CONFIG
- The BABE epoch configuration at genesis.
- [MAXIMUM_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAXIMUM_BLOCK_WEIGHT.html)- BLOCK_ - WEIGHT
- We allow for 2 seconds of compute with a 6 second average block time. The storage proof size is not limited so far.
- [NORMAL_](https://docs.rs/constant.NORMAL_DISPATCH_RATIO.html)- DISPATCH_ - RATIO
- We allow `Normal`extrinsics to fill up the block up to 75%, the rest can be used by Operational extrinsics.
- [RUNTIME_](https://docs.rs/constant.RUNTIME_API_VERSIONS.html)- API_ - VERSIONS
- [VERSION](https://docs.rs/constant.VERSION.html)
- Runtime version (Westend).
- [WASM_](https://docs.rs/constant.WASM_BINARY.html)- BINARY

# wipe_daemon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wipe-daemon/0.1.0/wipe_daemon/

## Expand description

The wipe local daemon: an `axum` server that exposes the board over HTTP/WS
and serves the embedded human UI. Started by `wipe serve`.

Collaboration remains git-only; this daemon is a *local* convenience for the
human UX. It records each served project in a machine-wide registry so the UI
can list every board you have opened.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AppState](https://docs.rs/struct.AppState.html)
- Shared server state.
- [Project](https://docs.rs/struct.ProjectEntry.html)- Entry
- One registered project.
- [Serve](https://docs.rs/struct.ServeConfig.html)- Config
- Configuration for a `wipe serve`invocation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_projects.html)- projects
- List all registered projects that still have a `.wipe`board, annotating each with its current board name.
- [serve](https://docs.rs/fn.serve.html)
- Start the daemon and serve until the process is stopped (Ctrl-C).

# wipe_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wipe-core/0.1.0/wipe_core/

## Expand description

Core storage engine and domain model for **wipe**.

`wipe-core` owns everything that touches a `.wipe` board on disk: the domain
model ([ model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)), deterministic JSON persistence and project discovery
(

[), stable ID formatting (](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)

`store`[), and the error type (](https://docs.rs/id/index.html)

`id`[).](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)

`error`Every mutation of a `.wipe` directory in the entire project MUST go through this
crate so that serialization stays deterministic (stable key order, trailing
newline, atomic writes) and git diffs remain minimal and merge-friendly.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error type shared across `wipe-core`.
- [git](https://docs.rs/git/index.html)
- Lightweight git integration by shelling out to the `git`CLI.
- [id](https://docs.rs/id/index.html)
- Stable, human-friendly ID formatting.
- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- The wipe domain model.
- [ops](https://docs.rs/ops/index.html)
- High-level, transactional board operations shared by every front-end
(CLI, daemon, desktop). Each function loads what it needs through `Store`
- [store](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)
- Deterministic, atomic persistence of a `.wipe`board and project discovery.

# sim_lib_numbers_tensor_i64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-tensor-i64/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_numbers_tensor_i64/

## Expand description

i64 tensor specialization: a contiguous `i64` tensor element type and its
`SpecTensor` backend, with overflow-checked operations that fall back to the
bigint domain.

[ I64Tensor](https://docs.rs/struct.I64Tensor.html) is the storage type (a flat

`i64` buffer); its checked
operations return an [that widens to bigint on overflow.](https://docs.rs/enum.I64AddResult.html)

`I64AddResult`[registers it as the](https://docs.rs/struct.I64TensorLib.html)

`I64TensorLib``i64` element-type backend for the base
tensor domain.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

In-range additions stay on the fast specialized path:

```
use sim_lib_numbers_tensor_i64::{I64Tensor, I64AddResult};
let tensor = I64Tensor::new(vec![3], vec![1, 2, 3]).unwrap();
assert!(matches!(
    tensor.checked_add_scalar(10),
    I64AddResult::Specialized(_)
));
```
Overflow widens the whole result into a bigint uniform tensor:

```
use sim_lib_numbers_tensor_i64::{I64Tensor, I64AddResult};
let tensor = I64Tensor::new(vec![2], vec![i64::MAX, 3]).unwrap();
assert!(matches!(
    tensor.checked_add_scalar(1),
    I64AddResult::Uniform(_)
));
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [I64Tensor](https://docs.rs/struct.I64Tensor.html)
- A tensor whose cells are native `i64`values in a contiguous buffer.
- [I64Tensor](https://docs.rs/struct.I64TensorLib.html)- Lib
- Registered library that installs the native-`i64`tensor backend.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [I64Add](https://docs.rs/enum.I64AddResult.html)- Result
- Outcome of an overflow-checked `i64`tensor operation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [tensor_](https://docs.rs/fn.tensor_lib_symbol.html)- lib_ - symbol
- The manifest id symbol for this library (`numbers/tensor-i64`).
- [tensor_](https://docs.rs/fn.tensor_spec_symbol.html)- spec_ - symbol
- The symbol under which the `i64`-tensor`SpecTensor`

# bp_bridge_hub_cumulus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bp-bridge-hub-cumulus/0.32.0/bp_bridge_hub_cumulus/

## Expand description

Primitives of all Cumulus-based bridge hubs.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Account](https://docs.rs/struct.AccountInfoStorageMapKeyProvider.html)- Info - Storage - MapKey - Provider
- Provides a storage key for account data.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockExecutionWeight.html)- Execution - Weight
- Importing a block with 0 Extrinsics.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockLength.html)- Length
- Size limit of the Cumulus-based bridge hub blocks.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockWeights.html)- Weights
- Weight limit of the Cumulus-based bridge hub blocks.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockWeightsForAsyncBacking.html)- Weights - ForAsync - Backing
- Weight limit of the Cumulus-based bridge hub blocks when async backing is enabled.
- [Extrinsic](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtrinsicBaseWeight.html)- Base - Weight
- Executing a NO-OP `System::remarks`Extrinsic.
- [Perbill](https://docs.rs/struct.Perbill.html)
- A fixed point representation of a number in the range [0, 1].

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [AVERAGE_](https://docs.rs/constant.AVERAGE_BLOCK_INTERVAL.html)- BLOCK_ - INTERVAL
- Average block time for Cumulus-based parachains
- [AVERAGE_](https://docs.rs/constant.AVERAGE_ON_INITIALIZE_RATIO.html)- ON_ - INITIALIZE_ - RATIO
- We assume that ~5% of the block weight is consumed by `on_initialize`handlers. This is used to limit the maximal weight of a single extrinsic.
- [EXTRA_](https://docs.rs/constant.EXTRA_STORAGE_PROOF_SIZE.html)- STORAGE_ - PROOF_ - SIZE
- Number of extra bytes (excluding size of storage value itself) of storage proof, built at Polkadot-like chain. This mostly depends on number of entries in the storage trie. Some reserve is reserved to account future chain growth.
- [MAXIMUM_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAXIMUM_BLOCK_WEIGHT.html)- BLOCK_ - WEIGHT
- We allow for 0.5 seconds of compute with a 6 second average block time.
- [MAXIMUM_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAXIMUM_BLOCK_WEIGHT_FOR_ASYNC_BACKING.html)- BLOCK_ - WEIGHT_ - FOR_ - ASYNC_ - BACKING
- We allow for 2 seconds of compute with a 6 second average block.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_ASSET_HUB_HEADER_SIZE.html)- ASSET_ - HUB_ - HEADER_ - SIZE
- Maximal asset hub header size.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_BRIDGE_HUB_HEADER_SIZE.html)- BRIDGE_ - HUB_ - HEADER_ - SIZE
- Maximal bridge hub header size.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_UNCONFIRMED_MESSAGES_IN_CONFIRMATION_TX.html)- UNCONFIRMED_ - MESSAGES_ - IN_ - CONFIRMATION_ - TX
- Maximal number of unconfirmed messages at inbound lane for Cumulus-based parachains. Note: this value is security-relevant, decreasing it should not be done without careful analysis (like the one above).
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_UNREWARDED_RELAYERS_IN_CONFIRMATION_TX.html)- UNREWARDED_ - RELAYERS_ - IN_ - CONFIRMATION_ - TX
- Maximal number of unrewarded relayer entries at inbound lane for Cumulus-based parachains. Note: this value is security-relevant, decreasing it should not be done without careful analysis (like the one above).
- [NORMAL_](https://docs.rs/constant.NORMAL_DISPATCH_RATIO.html)- DISPATCH_ - RATIO
- We allow `Normal`extrinsics to fill up the block up to 75%, the rest can be used by Operational extrinsics.
- [SLOT_](https://docs.rs/constant.SLOT_DURATION.html)- DURATION
- [TX_](https://docs.rs/constant.TX_EXTRA_BYTES.html)- EXTRA_ - BYTES
- Maximal number of bytes, included in the signed Polkadot-like transaction apart from the encoded call itself.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- Id of account on Polkadot-like chains.

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#guise)guise

A Mantine-inspired component library for [gpui](https://github.com/zed-industries/zed).

`guise` provides a themed palette, sizing tokens, and a growing set of
ready-to-use components built on gpui’s `RenderOnce` builder pattern.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use guise::prelude::*;
Stack::new().gap(Size::Md).child(
    Button::new("save", "Save").variant(Variant::Filled),
)
```
Install a [ Theme](https://docs.rs/theme/struct.Theme.html) once at startup, then read it from any component:

- Multiline text-editor building blocks.

- Feedback: components that communicate state to the user.
- [flex](https://docs.rs/flex/index.html)
- Flexbox layout primitives, for people who think in `Row`/`Column`/`Container`/`Expanded`(à la Flutter).
- [input](https://docs.rs/input/index.html)
- Form inputs.
- [layout](https://docs.rs/layout/index.html)
- Layout primitives: vertical `Stack``Group``Center``AppShell``Container``Space`
- [nav](https://docs.rs/nav/index.html)
- Navigation: components for moving around an app, plus a `StatusBar`
- [overlay](https://docs.rs/overlay/index.html)
- Overlays: floating UI that paints above the page.
- [panegroup](https://docs.rs/panegroup/index.html)
- `PaneGroup`— a recursive tree of- **tabbed**panes (splits contain tabs), the Zed / VS Code editor-group workspace model as a reusable gpui component.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Common imports for building with `guise`.
- [reactive](https://docs.rs/reactive/index.html)
- A lightweight, React-flavored state layer over gpui.
- [style](https://docs.rs/style/index.html)
- Shared visual variants. Mantine resolves a `(color, variant)`pair into a background / foreground / border triple that every interactive component (Button, Badge, ActionIcon, …) draws from. This is that resolver.
- [theme](https://docs.rs/theme/index.html)
- The theme: palette + sizing tokens + color scheme, exposed as a gpui
`Global`so any component can resolve themed values during render.

# utf8-ranges 1.0.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/utf8-ranges/1.0.5

**DEPRECATED:** This crate has been folded into the
[ regex-syntax](https://docs.rs/regex-syntax) and is now deprecated.

# utf8-ranges

This crate converts contiguous ranges of Unicode scalar values to UTF-8 byte ranges. This is useful when constructing byte based automata from Unicode. Stated differently, this lets one embed UTF-8 decoding as part of one's automaton.

Dual-licensed under MIT or the [UNLICENSE](http://unlicense.org).

### Documentation

### Example

This shows how to convert a scalar value range (e.g., the basic multilingual plane) to a sequence of byte based character classes.

```
extern crate utf8_ranges;
use Utf8Sequences;
```
The output:

```
[0-7F]
[C2-DF][80-BF]
[E0][A0-BF][80-BF]
[E1-EC][80-BF][80-BF]
[ED][80-9F][80-BF]
[EE-EF][80-BF][80-BF]
```
These ranges can then be used to build an automaton. Namely:

- Every arbitrary sequence of bytes matches exactly one of the sequences of ranges or none of them.
- Every match sequence of bytes is guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. (Erroneous encodings of surrogate codepoints in UTF-8 cannot match any of the byte ranges above.)

---

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/utf8-ranges/1.0.5/source/

                    utf8-ranges 1.0.5

                DEPRECATED. Use regex-syntax::utf8 submodule instead.

# utf8_ranges - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/utf8-ranges/1.0.5/target-redirect/utf8_ranges/

## Expand description

Crate `utf8-ranges` converts ranges of Unicode scalar values to equivalent
ranges of UTF-8 bytes. This is useful for constructing byte based automatons
that need to embed UTF-8 decoding.

See the documentation on the `Utf8Sequences` iterator for more details and
an example.

[§](https://docs.rs#wait-what-is-this)Wait, what is this?

This is simplest to explain with an example. Let’s say you wanted to test
whether a particular byte sequence was a Cyrillic character. One possible
scalar value range is `[0400-04FF]`. The set of allowed bytes for this
range can be expressed as a sequence of byte ranges:

This is simple enough: simply encode the boundaries, `0400` encodes to
`D0 80` and `04FF` encodes to `D3 BF`, and create ranges from each
corresponding pair of bytes: `D0` to `D3` and `80` to `BF`.

However, what if you wanted to add the Cyrillic Supplementary characters to
your range? Your range might then become `[0400-052F]`. The same procedure
as above doesn’t quite work because `052F` encodes to `D4 AF`. The byte ranges
you’d get from the previous transformation would be `[D0-D4][80-AF]`. However,
this isn’t quite correct because this range doesn’t capture many characters,
for example, `04FF` (because its last byte, `BF` isn’t in the range `80-AF`).

Instead, you need multiple sequences of byte ranges:

This gets even more complicated if you want bigger ranges, particularly if
they naively contain surrogate codepoints. For example, the sequence of byte
ranges for the basic multilingual plane (`[0000-FFFF]`) look like this:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
[0-7F]
[C2-DF][80-BF]
[E0][A0-BF][80-BF]
[E1-EC][80-BF][80-BF]
[ED][80-9F][80-BF]
[EE-EF][80-BF][80-BF]
```
Note that the byte ranges above will *not* match any erroneous encoding of
UTF-8, including encodings of surrogate codepoints.

And, of course, for all of Unicode (`[000000-10FFFF]`):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
[0-7F]
[C2-DF][80-BF]
[E0][A0-BF][80-BF]
[E1-EC][80-BF][80-BF]
[ED][80-9F][80-BF]
[EE-EF][80-BF][80-BF]
[F0][90-BF][80-BF][80-BF]
[F1-F3][80-BF][80-BF][80-BF]
[F4][80-8F][80-BF][80-BF]
```
This crate automates the process of creating these byte ranges from ranges of Unicode scalar values.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-would-i-ever-use-this)Why would I ever use this?

You probably won’t ever need this. In 99% of cases, you just decode the byte sequence into a Unicode scalar value and compare scalar values directly. However, this explicit decoding step isn’t always possible. For example, the construction of some finite state machines may benefit from converting ranges of scalar values into UTF-8 decoder automata (e.g., for character classes in regular expressions).

[§](https://docs.rs#lineage)Lineage

I got the idea and general implementation strategy from Russ Cox in his
[article on regexps](https://web.archive.org/web/20160404141123/https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp3.html) and RE2.
Russ Cox got it from Ken Thompson’s `grep` (no source, folk lore?).
I also got the idea from
[Lucene](https://github.com/apache/lucene-solr/blob/ae93f4e7ac6a3908046391de35d4f50a0d3c59ca/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/util/automaton/UTF32ToUTF8.java),
which uses it for executing automata on their term index.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Range.html)- Range
- A single inclusive range of UTF-8 bytes.
- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Sequences.html)- Sequences
- An iterator over ranges of matching UTF-8 byte sequences.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/enum.Utf8Sequence.html)- Sequence
- Utf8Sequence represents a sequence of byte ranges.

[104](https://docs.rs#104)
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// Utf8Sequence represents a sequence of byte ranges.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// To match a Utf8Sequence, a candidate byte sequence must match each
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// successive range.
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// For example, if there are two ranges, `[C2-DF][80-BF]`, then the byte
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// sequence `\xDD\x61` would not match because `0x61 < 0x80`.
[112](https://docs.rs#112)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Eq, PartialEq)]
[113](https://docs.rs#113)pub enum Utf8Sequence {
[114](https://docs.rs#114)    /// One byte range.
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    One(Utf8Range),
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// Two successive byte ranges.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    Two([Utf8Range; 2]),
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// Three successive byte ranges.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    Three([Utf8Range; 3]),
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    /// Four successive byte ranges.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    Four([Utf8Range; 4]),
[122](https://docs.rs#122)}
[123](https://docs.rs#123)
[124](https://docs.rs#124)impl Utf8Sequence {
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// Creates a new UTF-8 sequence from the encoded bytes of a scalar value
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// range.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    ///
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// This assumes that `start` and `end` have the same length.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    fn from_encoded_range(start: &[u8], end: &[u8]) -> Self {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        assert_eq!(start.len(), end.len());
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        match start.len() {
[132](https://docs.rs#132)            2 => Utf8Sequence::Two([
[133](https://docs.rs#133)                Utf8Range::new(start[0], end[0]),
[134](https://docs.rs#134)                Utf8Range::new(start[1], end[1]),
[135](https://docs.rs#135)            ]),
[136](https://docs.rs#136)            3 => Utf8Sequence::Three([
[137](https://docs.rs#137)                Utf8Range::new(start[0], end[0]),
[138](https://docs.rs#138)                Utf8Range::new(start[1], end[1]),
[139](https://docs.rs#139)                Utf8Range::new(start[2], end[2]),
[140](https://docs.rs#140)            ]),
[141](https://docs.rs#141)            4 => Utf8Sequence::Four([
[142](https://docs.rs#142)                Utf8Range::new(start[0], end[0]),
[143](https://docs.rs#143)                Utf8Range::new(start[1], end[1]),
[144](https://docs.rs#144)                Utf8Range::new(start[2], end[2]),
[145](https://docs.rs#145)                Utf8Range::new(start[3], end[3]),
[146](https://docs.rs#146)            ]),
[147](https://docs.rs#147)            n => unreachable!("invalid encoded length: {}", n),
[148](https://docs.rs#148)        }
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    }
[150](https://docs.rs#150)
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// Returns the underlying sequence of byte ranges as a slice.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    pub fn as_slice(&self) -> &[Utf8Range] {
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        use self::Utf8Sequence::*;
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        match *self {
[155](https://docs.rs#155)            One(ref r) => slice::from_ref(r),
[156](https://docs.rs#156)            Two(ref r) => &r[..],
[157](https://docs.rs#157)            Three(ref r) => &r[..],
[158](https://docs.rs#158)            Four(ref r) => &r[..],
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    /// Returns the number of byte ranges in this sequence.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    ///
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// The length is guaranteed to be in the closed interval `[1, 4]`.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        self.as_slice().len()
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// Returns true if and only if a prefix of `bytes` matches this sequence
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// of byte ranges.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    pub fn matches(&self, bytes: &[u8]) -> bool {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)        if bytes.len() < self.len() {
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            return false;
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        }
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        for (&b, r) in bytes.iter().zip(self) {
[176](https://docs.rs#176)            if !r.matches(b) {
[177](https://docs.rs#177)                return false;
[178](https://docs.rs#178)            }
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        }
[180](https://docs.rs#180)        true
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    }
[182](https://docs.rs#182)}
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)impl<'a> IntoIterator for &'a Utf8Sequence {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    type IntoIter = slice::Iter<'a, Utf8Range>;
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    type Item = &'a Utf8Range;
[187](https://docs.rs#187)
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    fn into_iter(self) -> Self::IntoIter {
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        self.as_slice().into_iter()
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    }
[191](https://docs.rs#191)}
[192](https://docs.rs#192)
[193](https://docs.rs#193)impl fmt::Debug for Utf8Sequence {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        use self::Utf8Sequence::*;
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        match *self {
[197](https://docs.rs#197)            One(ref r) => write!(f, "{:?}", r),
[198](https://docs.rs#198)            Two(ref r) => write!(f, "{:?}{:?}", r[0], r[1]),
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            Three(ref r) => write!(f, "{:?}{:?}{:?}", r[0], r[1], r[2]),
[200](https://docs.rs#200)            Four(ref r) => write!(f, "{:?}{:?}{:?}{:?}",
[201](https://docs.rs#201)                                  r[0], r[1], r[2], r[3]),
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        }
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)}
[205](https://docs.rs#205)
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// A single inclusive range of UTF-8 bytes.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[208](https://docs.rs#208)pub struct Utf8Range {
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// Start of byte range (inclusive).
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    pub start: u8,
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// End of byte range (inclusive).
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    pub end: u8,
[213](https://docs.rs#213)}
[214](https://docs.rs#214)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)impl Utf8Range {
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    fn new(start: u8, end: u8) -> Self {
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        Utf8Range { start: start, end: end }
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    }
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    /// Returns true if and only if the given byte is in this range.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    pub fn matches(&self, b: u8) -> bool {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)        self.start <= b && b <= self.end
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    }
[224](https://docs.rs#224)}
[225](https://docs.rs#225)
[226](https://docs.rs#226)impl fmt::Debug for Utf8Range {
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        if self.start == self.end {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)            write!(f, "[{:X}]", self.start)
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        } else {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            write!(f, "[{:X}-{:X}]", self.start, self.end)
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    }
[234](https://docs.rs#234)}
[235](https://docs.rs#235)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)/// An iterator over ranges of matching UTF-8 byte sequences.
[237](https://docs.rs#237)///
[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// The iteration represents an alternation of comprehensive byte sequences
[239](https://docs.rs#239)/// that match precisely the set of UTF-8 encoded scalar values.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)///
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// A byte sequence corresponds to one of the scalar values in the range given
[242](https://docs.rs#242)/// if and only if it completely matches exactly one of the sequences of byte
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// ranges produced by this iterator.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)///
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// Each sequence of byte ranges matches a unique set of bytes. That is, no two
[246](https://docs.rs#246)/// sequences will match the same bytes.
[247](https://docs.rs#247)///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)/// # Example
[249](https://docs.rs#249)///
[250](https://docs.rs#250)/// This shows how to match an arbitrary byte sequence against a range of
[251](https://docs.rs#251)/// scalar values.
[252](https://docs.rs#252)///
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// ```rust
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// use utf8_ranges::{Utf8Sequences, Utf8Sequence};
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// fn matches(seqs: &[Utf8Sequence], bytes: &[u8]) -> bool {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)///     for range in seqs {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///         if range.matches(bytes) {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)///             return true;
[260](https://docs.rs#260)///         }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)///     }
[262](https://docs.rs#262)///     false
[263](https://docs.rs#263)/// }
[264](https://docs.rs#264)///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)/// // Test the basic multilingual plane.
[266](https://docs.rs#266)/// let seqs: Vec<_> = Utf8Sequences::new('\u{0}', '\u{FFFF}').collect();
[267](https://docs.rs#267)///
[268](https://docs.rs#268)/// // UTF-8 encoding of 'a'.
[269](https://docs.rs#269)/// assert!(matches(&seqs, &[0x61]));
[270](https://docs.rs#270)/// // UTF-8 encoding of '☃' (`\u{2603}`).
[271](https://docs.rs#271)/// assert!(matches(&seqs, &[0xE2, 0x98, 0x83]));
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// // UTF-8 encoding of `\u{10348}` (outside the BMP).
[273](https://docs.rs#273)/// assert!(!matches(&seqs, &[0xF0, 0x90, 0x8D, 0x88]));
[274](https://docs.rs#274)/// // Tries to match against a UTF-8 encoding of a surrogate codepoint,
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// // which is invalid UTF-8, and therefore fails, despite the fact that
[276](https://docs.rs#276)/// // the corresponding codepoint (0xD800) falls in the range given.
[277](https://docs.rs#277)/// assert!(!matches(&seqs, &[0xED, 0xA0, 0x80]));
[278](https://docs.rs#278)/// // And fails against plain old invalid UTF-8.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)/// assert!(!matches(&seqs, &[0xFF, 0xFF]));
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// ```
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)/// If this example seems circuitous, that's because it is! It's meant to be
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// illustrative. In practice, you could just try to decode your byte sequence
[284](https://docs.rs#284)/// and compare it with the scalar value range directly. However, this is not
[285](https://docs.rs#285)/// always possible (for example, in a byte based automaton).
[286](https://docs.rs#286)pub struct Utf8Sequences {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    range_stack: Vec<ScalarRange>,
[288](https://docs.rs#288)}
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)impl Utf8Sequences {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    /// Create a new iterator over UTF-8 byte ranges for the scalar value range
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// given.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    pub fn new(start: char, end: char) -> Self {
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        let mut it = Utf8Sequences { range_stack: vec![] };
[295](https://docs.rs#295)        it.push(start as u32, end as u32);
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        it
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    }
[298](https://docs.rs#298)
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    /// reset resets the scalar value range.
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// Any existing state is cleared, but resources may be reused.
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    ///
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// N.B. Benchmarks say that this method is dubious.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    #[doc(hidden)]
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    pub fn reset(&mut self, start: char, end: char) {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)        self.range_stack.clear();
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        self.push(start as u32, end as u32);
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    }
[308](https://docs.rs#308)
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    fn push(&mut self, start: u32, end: u32) {
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        self.range_stack.push(ScalarRange { start: start, end: end });
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    }
[312](https://docs.rs#312)}
[313](https://docs.rs#313)
[314](https://docs.rs#314)struct ScalarRange {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    start: u32,
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    end: u32,
[317](https://docs.rs#317)}
[318](https://docs.rs#318)
[319](https://docs.rs#319)impl fmt::Debug for ScalarRange {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        write!(f, "ScalarRange({:X}, {:X})", self.start, self.end)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    }
[323](https://docs.rs#323)}
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)impl Iterator for Utf8Sequences {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    type Item = Utf8Sequence;
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    'TOP:
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        while let Some(mut r) = self.range_stack.pop() {
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        'INNER:
[332](https://docs.rs#332)            loop {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                if let Some((r1, r2)) = r.split() {
[334](https://docs.rs#334)                    self.push(r2.start, r2.end);
[335](https://docs.rs#335)                    r.start = r1.start;
[336](https://docs.rs#336)                    r.end = r1.end;
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                    continue 'INNER;
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                }
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                if !r.is_valid() {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                    continue 'TOP;
[341](https://docs.rs#341)                }
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                for i in 1..MAX_UTF8_BYTES {
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                    let max = max_scalar_value(i);
[344](https://docs.rs#344)                    if r.start <= max && max < r.end {
[345](https://docs.rs#345)                        self.push(max + 1, r.end);
[346](https://docs.rs#346)                        r.end = max;
[347](https://docs.rs#347)                        continue 'INNER;
[348](https://docs.rs#348)                    }
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                }
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                if let Some(ascii_range) = r.as_ascii() {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                    return Some(Utf8Sequence::One(ascii_range));
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                }
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                for i in 1..MAX_UTF8_BYTES {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)                    let m = (1 << (6 * i)) - 1;
[355](https://docs.rs#355)                    if (r.start & !m) != (r.end & !m) {
[356](https://docs.rs#356)                        if (r.start & m) != 0 {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)                            self.push((r.start | m) + 1, r.end);
[358](https://docs.rs#358)                            r.end = r.start | m;
[359](https://docs.rs#359)                            continue 'INNER;
[360](https://docs.rs#360)                        }
[361](https://docs.rs#361)                        if (r.end & m) != m {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)                            self.push(r.end & !m, r.end);
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                            r.end = (r.end & !m) - 1;
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                            continue 'INNER;
[365](https://docs.rs#365)                        }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)                    }
[367](https://docs.rs#367)                }
[368](https://docs.rs#368)                let mut start = [0; MAX_UTF8_BYTES];
[369](https://docs.rs#369)                let mut end = [0; MAX_UTF8_BYTES];
[370](https://docs.rs#370)                let n = r.encode(&mut start, &mut end);
[371](https://docs.rs#371)                return Some(Utf8Sequence::from_encoded_range(
[372](https://docs.rs#372)                    &start[0..n], &end[0..n]));
[373](https://docs.rs#373)            }
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        }
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        None
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    }
[377](https://docs.rs#377)}
[378](https://docs.rs#378)
[379](https://docs.rs#379)impl ScalarRange {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// split splits this range if it overlaps with a surrogate codepoint.
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    ///
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// Either or both ranges may be invalid.
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    fn split(&self) -> Option<(ScalarRange, ScalarRange)> {
[384](https://docs.rs#384)        if self.start < 0xE000 && self.end > 0xD7FF {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)            Some((ScalarRange {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)                start: self.start,
[387](https://docs.rs#387)                end: 0xD7FF,
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            }, ScalarRange {
[389](https://docs.rs#389)                start: 0xE000,
[390](https://docs.rs#390)                end: self.end,
[391](https://docs.rs#391)            }))
[392](https://docs.rs#392)        } else {
[393](https://docs.rs#393)            None
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        }
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    }
[396](https://docs.rs#396)
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// is_valid returns true if and only if start <= end.
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    fn is_valid(&self) -> bool {
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        self.start <= self.end
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    }
[401](https://docs.rs#401)
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// as_ascii returns this range as a Utf8Range if and only if all scalar
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// values in this range can be encoded as a single byte.
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    fn as_ascii(&self) -> Option<Utf8Range> {
[405](https://docs.rs#405)        if self.is_ascii() {
[406](https://docs.rs#406)            Some(Utf8Range::new(self.start as u8, self.end as u8))
[407](https://docs.rs#407)        } else {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)            None
[409](https://docs.rs#409)        }
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    }
[411](https://docs.rs#411)
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// is_ascii returns true if the range is ASCII only (i.e., takes a single
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// byte to encode any scalar value).
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    fn is_ascii(&self) -> bool {
[415](https://docs.rs#415)        self.is_valid() && self.end <= 0x7f
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    }
[417](https://docs.rs#417)
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// encode writes the UTF-8 encoding of the start and end of this range
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// to the corresponding destination slices.
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    ///
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// The slices should have room for at least `MAX_UTF8_BYTES`.
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    fn encode(&self, start: &mut [u8], end: &mut [u8]) -> usize {
[423](https://docs.rs#423)        let cs = char::from_u32(self.start).unwrap();
[424](https://docs.rs#424)        let ce = char::from_u32(self.end).unwrap();
[425](https://docs.rs#425)        let n = encode_utf8(cs, start).unwrap();
[426](https://docs.rs#426)        let m = encode_utf8(ce, end).unwrap();
[427](https://docs.rs#427)        assert_eq!(n, m);
[428](https://docs.rs#428)        n
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    }
[430](https://docs.rs#430)}
[431](https://docs.rs#431)
[432](https://docs.rs#432)fn max_scalar_value(nbytes: usize) -> u32 {
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    match nbytes {
[434](https://docs.rs#434)        1 => 0x007F,
[435](https://docs.rs#435)        2 => 0x07FF,
[436](https://docs.rs#436)        3 => 0xFFFF,
[437](https://docs.rs#437)        4 => 0x10FFFF,
[438](https://docs.rs#438)        _ => unreachable!("invalid UTF-8 byte sequence size"),
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    }
[440](https://docs.rs#440)}
[441](https://docs.rs#441)
[442](https://docs.rs#442)#[cfg(test)]
[443](https://docs.rs#443)mod tests {
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    use std::char;
[445](https://docs.rs#445)
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    use quickcheck::{TestResult, quickcheck};
[447](https://docs.rs#447)
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    use {Utf8Range, Utf8Sequences};
[449](https://docs.rs#449)
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    fn rutf8(s: u8, e: u8) -> Utf8Range {
[451](https://docs.rs#451)        Utf8Range::new(s, e)
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    }
[453](https://docs.rs#453)
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    fn never_accepts_surrogate_codepoints(start: char, end: char) {
[455](https://docs.rs#455)        for cp in 0xD800..0xE000 {
[456](https://docs.rs#456)            let buf = encode_surrogate(cp);
[457](https://docs.rs#457)            for r in Utf8Sequences::new(start, end) {
[458](https://docs.rs#458)                if r.matches(&buf) {
[459](https://docs.rs#459)                    panic!(
[460](https://docs.rs#460)                        "Sequence ({:X}, {:X}) contains range {:?}, \
[461](https://docs.rs#461)                         which matches surrogate code point {:X} \
[462](https://docs.rs#462)                         with encoded bytes {:?}",
[463](https://docs.rs#463)                        start as u32, end as u32, r, cp, buf,

# Utf8Sequences in utf8_ranges - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/utf8-ranges/1.0.5/utf8_ranges/struct.Utf8Sequences.html

`pub struct Utf8Sequences { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An iterator over ranges of matching UTF-8 byte sequences.

The iteration represents an alternation of comprehensive byte sequences that match precisely the set of UTF-8 encoded scalar values.

A byte sequence corresponds to one of the scalar values in the range given if and only if it completely matches exactly one of the sequences of byte ranges produced by this iterator.

Each sequence of byte ranges matches a unique set of bytes. That is, no two sequences will match the same bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This shows how to match an arbitrary byte sequence against a range of scalar values.

```
use utf8_ranges::{Utf8Sequences, Utf8Sequence};
fn matches(seqs: &[Utf8Sequence], bytes: &[u8]) -> bool {
    for range in seqs {
        if range.matches(bytes) {
            return true;
        }
    }
    false
}
// Test the basic multilingual plane.
let seqs: Vec<_> = Utf8Sequences::new('\u{0}', '\u{FFFF}').collect();
// UTF-8 encoding of 'a'.
assert!(matches(&seqs, &[0x61]));
// UTF-8 encoding of '☃' (`\u{2603}`).
assert!(matches(&seqs, &[0xE2, 0x98, 0x83]));
// UTF-8 encoding of `\u{10348}` (outside the BMP).
assert!(!matches(&seqs, &[0xF0, 0x90, 0x8D, 0x88]));
// Tries to match against a UTF-8 encoding of a surrogate codepoint,
// which is invalid UTF-8, and therefore fails, despite the fact that
// the corresponding codepoint (0xD800) falls in the range given.
assert!(!matches(&seqs, &[0xED, 0xA0, 0x80]));
// And fails against plain old invalid UTF-8.
assert!(!matches(&seqs, &[0xFF, 0xFF]));
```
If this example seems circuitous, that’s because it is! It’s meant to be illustrative. In practice, you could just try to decode your byte sequence and compare it with the scalar value range directly. However, this is not always possible (for example, in a byte based automaton).
